threatModelSummary: This change adds a local, offline test fixture (static HTML/JS page), a path-bounded static file server for Playwright's webServer, and a browser-side helper (fixture.ts) that loads @turf/turf from a local file path instead of a CDN. The spec's own Trust Boundaries section ('None — no auth, no user input, no external calls') matches what the code shows: no authentication, no session/token handling, no user-facing API endpoint, and no network calls once the suite is running (AC4 runs it with --network none). The only new code that parses request-shaped input is fixtures/serve.mjs's route resolution, which is local-only test infrastructure never shipped in dist/. I verified its path-traversal guard empirically (encoded and raw '..' traversal attempts against both routes returned 404) rather than relying on inspection alone. The new runtime dependency, @turf/turf, was checked against the full dependency tree via pnpm audit and introduces no vulnerabilities. No fixes were required; no files were modified during this review.
dependencyAudit: pnpm audit --prod run against the full monorepo: 33 pre-existing findings (2 low, 15 moderate, 14 high, 2 critical), none in a dependency path through @turf/turf, @types/leaflet, leaflet, or packages/saturday-playwright-leaflet. All findings trace to apps/cartridge, apps/mock-api, and packages/saturday-cucumber-otel-formatter, which this feature did not touch.

@turf/turf ^6.5.0 added to dependencies (not devDependencies) because fixture.ts loads its browser bundle into the page under test at runtime — same category leaflet is already in. No advisory applies to this version per the audit above.

stride.assessed: No authentication or identity concept exists anywhere in this feature. fixtures/serve.mjs serves static files with no session, cookie, or credential handling — there is nothing to spoof.

The only request-driven code path is serve.mjs's resolveRequestedFile/resolveWithinRoot, which resolves a request path against a fixed root and rejects anything that escapes it. Verified empirically: encoded ('..%2f'), raw ('../'), and cross-route traversal attempts against both the '/leaflet/' and '/assets/' routes all returned 404. The '/' and '/turf.min.js' routes are exact-match against fixed, non-user-controlled paths with no request input involved.
Not applicable — no user actions, no audit-worthy operations. This is a test fixture with no concept of a user performing an action that would need non-repudiation.

serve.mjs's allow-listed routes only ever expose node_modules/leaflet/dist, the package's own fixtures/assets/ directory, and node_modules/@turf/turf/turf.min.js — no secrets, source code outside those two directories, or environment data are reachable even via the traversal attempts tested. The page itself (fixture-map.js) hardcodes fixture coordinates and popup text with no real user or system data. Egress: nothing in this feature makes an outbound network call — AC4 explicitly runs the suite with --network none, and the browser-side code loads Leaflet/Turf/image assets from the local server only.

serve.mjs is a local-only server bound for the duration of a test run (default port 4173), not a long-running or internet-facing service. No unbounded loops over external input; file reads are a single readFile per request with no size cap, but inputs are limited to the fixed asset set this package ships, not arbitrary user-supplied data. Not in scope as a hardening target given its test-infra-only lifecycle.
No roles, permissions, or privilege levels exist in this feature — there is nothing to elevate into.

The empirical traversal check (encoded '..%2f', raw '../', cross-route) against fixtures/serve.mjs is documented here for the record; QA does not need to re-run it as a dedicated test since it's test-only local infrastructure with no production exposure, but it's safe to reuse these exact curl invocations if a regression test for the server itself is ever desired.
